t: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet — Filter Overshooters, Then Match Coordinates
o: One operation replaces a triplet by the componentwise max of itself and another triplet, applied any number of times; we ask whether target can appear among the triplets. Example 1: merging [2,5,3] into [1,7,5] yields exactly [2,7,5]. Example 2 fails because no triplet can ever supply the required 2 in the middle slot. Example 3 shows different coordinates may come from different donors: 5 from the fourth triplet (first slot), 5 from the second (middle), 5 from the third (last). Since max never decreases any component, any triplet containing a value ABOVE its matching target coordinate is poison — merging it in would overshoot that coordinate permanently.
k: Merging is componentwise max, so values only grow: a triplet with any component exceeding its target counterpart must never be used.
Among safe triplets the merge order is irrelevant — max is commutative and idempotent — so the best reachable state is the componentwise max of ALL safe triplets combined.
Hence target is achievable iff each of x, y, z appears as some safe triplet's matching coordinate, checkable in one linear pass.

a.i: Keep one working triplet and repeatedly sweep the list, absorbing every safe triplet (no component above target) that improves some coordinate. Components rise monotonically and are capped by target, so the process terminates at the componentwise max over all safe triplets — exactly the best achievable state. This mirrors how one would actually play the operations and is easy to reason about, but it rescans the whole list on every improving round.
s: Start with cur = null and repeat sweeps until nothing changes.
Each sweep: skip unsafe triplets (any component above target's).
Seed cur with the first safe triplet seen; otherwise raise every cur coordinate that a safe triplet beats.
After each sweep return true immediately if cur equals target.
When a full sweep improves nothing, return whether cur hit target.
a.t: O(n x s) where s counts productive sweeps — bounded by the number of distinct coordinate upgrades, so small in practice though not strictly linear.

a.i: Two observations collapse everything: unsafe triplets (some component above the target's) can never participate, and among safe ones order does not matter because max merges commute. Therefore just verify that the safe pool contains, per coordinate, at least one triplet supplying exactly x, y, or z. One pass with three boolean flags answers the question.
s: Scan all triplets; skip any with t[0] > x or t[1] > y or t[2] > z.
For surviving triplets set foundX if t[0] == x, foundY if t[1] == y, foundZ if t[2] == z.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan with constant work per triplet.
a.sp: O(1) — three flags (or a small set of at most three labels).

w: Recognize the max-only-grows invariant early — it instantly kills overshooting triplets and dissolves the sequencing question entirely, since merged maxes commute. Pitfalls: searching for a single triplet equal to target (wrong — coordinates may come from different donors, as Example 3 shows), and forgetting to filter overshooters before reasoning about reachability. Edge cases: target already present in the list (true with zero operations); duplicate coordinate values in target are handled naturally by separate flags. Follow-up: output an explicit merge schedule (remember which safe triplet supplied each winning coordinate, then chain the merges).
